ann_80.text: Through this part, an international plan clearly raises the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving from about 3% to about 24%, and more voice-mail messages (0 to 32) clearly raise it to about 13%.
A voice-mail plan slightly lowers it to below 1%, and more night-time minutes slightly raise it to about 3%.
Being in Montana, Oregon or Washington rather than West Virginia raises it to about 8% to 10% (on the training data only).

South Carolina slightly raises it to about 7%, New Jersey, Louisiana and Alaska to about 5% and Indiana, Maryland, Arizona, Wisconsin, Florida, Alabama and the states this part does not single out to about 3% to 4%, while Vermont and Wyoming slightly lower it to about 1% and Utah, Virginia, Missouri, Georgia, Washington DC and Pennsylvania to about 2% (on the training data only).
More international and evening minutes slightly raise it, while more international calls and a higher night-time charge slightly lower it (on the training data only).

ann_81.text: Through this part, customer-service calls clearly raise the predicted chance of leaving, and even more so in Oregon: going from 0 to 3 calls moves it from below 1% to about 18% there, against about 2% to about 5% elsewhere.
For the typical customer, customer-service calls (0 to 3) slightly raise it from about 2% to about 5%.

More daytime minutes slightly raise it to about 4%, less so in Oregon (from about 2% to about 4% there, against about 2% to about 9% elsewhere), and being in Oregon slightly lowers it to below 1% (on the training data only).
For a typical customer in Ohio, daytime minutes slightly add to it only once they rise above about 85 minutes, from about 2% to about 7% (on the training data only).

ann_82.text: Through this part, daytime minutes clearly add to the predicted chance of leaving only once they rise above about 234 minutes: for the typical customer, going from 0 to 271 minutes moves it from about 3% to about 17%.

Daytime minutes clearly raise it, and even more so for customers with more than 201 evening minutes: going from 112 to 249 minutes moves it from about 2% to about 21%, against about 2% to about 4% otherwise.

This part acts on 747 of 4000 customers, 269 of whom left, and clearly raises the typical one's chance (a customer in Alabama with about 249 daytime minutes and 232 evening minutes) from about 5% to about 23%.
For that customer, more evening minutes (138 to 266) clearly raise it from about 5% to about 45%.
For the typical customer, more daytime minutes across the usual range slightly raise it, from about 3% to about 6%.

ann_83.text: Through this part, the daytime charge slightly adds to the predicted chance of leaving only once it rises above about 39.72 US dollars, staying at about 3% for the typical customer (on the training data only).
Being in Rhode Island or Michigan slightly lowers it (on the training data only).

ann_84.text: Through this part, being in South Dakota or Utah slightly raises the predicted chance of leaving to about 7% and Maine to about 5%, while Hawaii and Alaska slightly lower it to about 1% or below (on the training data only).
This part acts on 3845 of 4000 customers, and for the typical one it slightly lowers the chance from about 7% to about 3% (on the training data only).

ann_85.text: Through this part, an area code other than 415 and being in Washington slightly raise the predicted chance of leaving, staying at about 3% (on the training data only).

It slightly widens the Washington effect outside area code 415: across the model, being in Washington raises the chance from about 3% to about 14% there, against about 3% to about 10% in area code 415.

ann_86.text: Through this part, a longer account (48 to 152) slightly raises the predicted chance of leaving from about 2% to about 3% (on the training data only).

ann_87.text: Across the whole model, an international plan clearly raises the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving from about 3% to about 24%, more voice-mail messages (0 to 32) clearly raise it to about 13% and more daytime minutes (112 to 249) clearly raise it from about 2% to about 9%.
Being in Montana, Washington or South Dakota rather than West Virginia raises it to about 9% to 10% (on the training data only).
